title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

When do identities become political — and does culture explain anything that economics has not already explained?


Chapter 3 left political culture sitting as the intervening step between economic change and political change. Chapter 4 asks whether it can carry that weight, or whether it is a residual we reach for when structure runs out.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 4, pp. 89–117.
Two halves to the chapter, and they are easy to lose track of. The first half is a concept under attack: political culture as attitudes, then three waves of criticism, then a renaissance. The second half is ethnicity and nationalism, which arrives because by the era of multiculturalism “culture” had come to be used interchangeably with ethnicity.
Keep the stakes in view: both halves end up at the same question, which is whether a society’s identities make democracy harder.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class you should be able to:

State Almond and Verba’s definition of political culture and place a country in Table 4.1
Say what the civic culture is a mix of, and why the mix matters more than any single type
Rehearse the three criticisms — definition, explanatory power, and production — and the best answer to each
Explain post-materialism, how it is measured, and what the measurement critique shows
Distinguish primordial from constructivist accounts of ethnicity
Use Greenfeld’s two dimensions to classify a nationalism
Separate fractionalization from polarization in the diversity-and-democracy debate

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: What is political culture?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Older than political science
Political culture is, at bottom, “the basic values, ideas, beliefs, attitudes, and orientations about politics” — what is right and wrong, acceptable and unacceptable, in political life.

Max Weber argued the values of Protestantism — hard work, honesty, seriousness, monetary thrift and efficiency — were especially conducive to the accumulation of capital, and so to capitalism and eventually democracy.

A comparative study: Buddhism, Catholicism, Confucianism, Islam
Other societies had some of these values; none had them all


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 89–90; Weber on the Protestant ethic.
The move that matters for us is that Weber’s claim was comparative in structure — he did not study Protestantism alone, he studied it against four alternatives. That is the standard the next generation failed to meet.
Weber’s extra wrinkle: accumulating wealth through commerce and usury — previously frowned on by the Catholic Church — came to signify that one was viewed favourably in the eyes of God.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Landes: the valuing of science
David Landes (1998) asks why industrialization came first to northern Europe — England, Germany, the Netherlands, Scandinavia.
His answer is cultural, but a different culture:

A valuing of science
Respect for autonomous intellectual inquiry
An emphasis on empiricism — itself growing out of the Protestant emphasis on the observable as proof of God’s favour



These values drove scientific and technological innovation from the Renaissance onward, laying the intellectual groundwork for the Industrial Revolution.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The war that made the field — and its flaw
text:
The war that made the field — and its flaw
As Wiarda (1999) notes, political culture studies were boosted by World War II.

Ruth Benedict (1934; The Chrysanthemum and the Sword, 1954)
Margaret Mead (1964)
Nathan Leites (1951)


Several were commissioned by the US government — first against Japan, then against the Soviet Union.



They did study attitudes toward power, hierarchy and duty. But they were non-comparative, single-country studies, emphasizing what was unique to each culture — which gave political scientists no general method.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 90.
This is a methodological point disguised as a history lesson, and it is worth naming as such in class — it is exactly Lijphart’s complaint from Session 1. A rich single-country description is not an explanation, because nothing varies.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The breakthrough: The Civic Culture (1963)
Gabriel Almond and Sidney Verba did two things the anthropologists had not.

Built a framework for systematic comparison across countries, instead of letting patterns “emerge”
Answered the question the earlier literature had dodged: beliefs and attitudes about what?



Political culture is “a set of specifically political orientations — attitudes toward the political system and its part and attitudes towards the role of the self in the system.”
Almond and Verba 1963, p. 12


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 90–91; Almond and Verba (1963, p. 12).
Two components in that definition, and the whole chapter turns on them: orientations (the psychological side) and objects (what the orientations are about). The objects are the parts of the political system as the structural-functionalist approach of Chapter 1 identified them — input processes, output processes, structures of the system.
Flag now, pay off later: the clause “the role of the self in the system” is precisely what Lijphart will call concept stretching.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three orientations







Cognitive
Knowledge of and belief about the political system, its roles, the incumbents of those roles, inputs and outputs


Affective
Feelings about the political system, its roles, personnel and performance


Evaluational
Judgments and opinions about political objects — typically combining value judgments or feelings with information





Note that evaluation is not a separate kind of thing but a combination: feeling plus information.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Four system dimensions
Each of the three orientations can be directed at four different objects:

The system as a whole — constitutional characteristics, political structures
The policy process — input objects, e.g. interest groups, parties
Policy enforcement — how policy is implemented; output objects
The self — does the individual perceive themselves as a member of the system, with a positive impact on it?



Collapse dimensions 2, 3 and 4 into a plus or a minus and you get the three political culture types.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 91–92.
Students read Table 4.1 as arbitrary unless they see that it is generated by this list. Build it on the board: system, input, output, self — four columns, and only three of the sixteen logical combinations get names.

[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, Table 4.1, after Almond and Verba (1963).
Worth saying out loud: the subject row is the interesting one, because it is positive on the system and on outputs but negative on inputs and self. That is a citizen who consumes government and does not make it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Parochial
Citizens are only remotely aware of a central government, and live their lives regardless of what the state decides.

Know little or nothing of the system, its parts, its processes
Do not believe they should participate
Do not expect to be beneficiaries of policy
See no role for the self



The old Russian peasant proverb: “God is high above and the Tsar is far away.”



Predominates in relatively poor, underdeveloped, agrarian societies where orientations are local rather than national — but parochials can be found in any society.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Subject
People know the system and something of how it works, but see themselves as subjects to authority.

Positively oriented to outputs — employment, education, healthcare — which they are quite willing to consume
Not oriented to inputs; no belief in a role for the self
Do not think they can or should articulate interests, aggregate them, or enter the policy process



Dominant in modern authoritarian states — the Soviet Union, Nazi Germany — where citizen activities are defined as duties rather than rights, and where the regime rests on performance legitimacy: as long as the outputs keep coming, people stay loyal.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 92–93.
The performance-legitimacy point is the one with the most mileage for their dossiers. It is also the bridge to Chapter 3: a subject culture plus a growth record is a stable authoritarianism, and a subject culture plus a recession is a crisis.
Such regimes often ground their right to rule in some ubiquitous “law of history” that only the political elite can interpret.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Participant
Individuals who know a great deal about the system, are positively oriented to both inputs and outputs, and believe they have a positive role to play.

They want to participate and to receive the benefits of policy
Found in modern, developed, wealthy societies with high mass literacy and education



Almond and Verba’s 1963 expectation: as a result of modernization, the world could be expected to become more participant.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 93.
That last sentence is modernization theory from Chapter 3, restated at the level of attitudes. Ask whether the sixty years since have borne it out — and what evidence would settle it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Ideal types, individually held, nationally mixed
text:
Ideal types, individually held, nationally mixed
Three things Almond and Verba insist on, all of which students skip:

These are ideal types — idealized characterizations, not descriptions of real societies
The attitudes are held at the individual level
Aggregated to the nation, every country is a mix of all three



So the comparative question is never “which type is this country.” It is what is the relative mix — in some the parochial impulse predominates, in others the participant.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The civic culture is a mix, not a maximum
text:
The civic culture is a mix, not a maximum

The mix that best supports stable democracy — the civic culture — is a majority of participants, tempered by a significant minority of subjects and some parochials.


From interviews with over 5,000 people across five countries, conducted over five years:

Great Britain and the United States — highest proportion of participants
Germany and Italy — highest proportion of subjects, consistent with their recent emergence from totalitarianism
Mexico — least democratic, greatest number of subjects and parochials


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 93–94; Almond and Verba (1963).
Do not let the headline finding pass without the footnote: Almond and Verba expressed concern that the proportion of participants in the United States was too high, and presented a destabilizing element in American politics. That is counter-intuitive enough to be memorable, and it is the whole reason the civic culture is defined as a tempered mix rather than a maximum.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what is the civic culture?
text:
Check: what is the civic culture?
Almond and Verba’s civic culture consists of:

Participants only
A majority of participants, tempered by some subjects and parochials
An equal share of all three types
A majority of subjects with a participant elite



A majority of participants, tempered by a significant minority of subjects and some parochials. Too many participants was itself a destabilizing element — which is why the answer is a mix and not a maximum.


[Key] Option 2. “Participants only” is the trap, because it is what the word “civic” suggests and what students assume the theory must want.
If someone picks option 1, the follow-up question is: what would a polity of nothing but participants look like? Almond and Verba’s worry was overload — every demand pressed at once, with nobody willing to defer.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Elazar: three American political cultures
Daniel Elazar (1972, 1994) applies the same logic inside one country, focusing on how people perceive the role of government.







Moral
Social concerns outweigh the individual; government a positive force; the commonwealth conception; politics as one of the great activities of man in search of the good society; issues matter; politicians are not to profit; more amateur participation


Individual
Government largely an impediment, to be restricted so as not to interfere with private activity; its role confined to encouraging private initiative; private concerns outweigh public


Traditional
Social and family ties prominent; emphasis on traditional hierarchies; government has a positive role but limited to maintaining the existing social order; leaders custodial rather than innovative




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 94–95; Elazar (1994, pp. 230–235).
Useful for a Texas classroom: Elazar’s own mapping puts Texas in the traditionalistic-individualistic band. Ask students which of the three they recognize in state politics, and what evidence they would cite — this is a low-stakes rehearsal of the claim-evidence map.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Three criticisms

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The three lines of attack


Definition — is the concept coherent, or stretched past usefulness?
Explanatory power — can culture be an independent variable at all?
Production — what explains where political cultures come from?



Together these drove the concept into decline. Each one also produced the repair that brought it back.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Criticism 1: the concept is stretched
Arend Lijphart (1980) is sympathetic — political culture is a powerful explanatory variable — but argues Almond and Verba stretched it.

Beyond orientations toward the political system, into general social and personal relations
Specifically, “the role of the self in the system”
The result is an unnecessary vagueness



His repair: focus entirely on how politics is conducted, not on feelings about the self and how the self interacts with others.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 95–96; Lijphart (1980).
Same Lijphart as Session 1, and the same instinct: a concept that travels too far stops discriminating between cases. Worth naming the continuity explicitly — students treat the Lijphart of the comparative method and the Lijphart of consociationalism as two different people.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Lijphart’s replacement: how decisions get made
text:
Lijphart’s replacement: how decisions get made







Consensual
Political decisions should maximize the number of points of view represented; consensus among them should be achieved; societal differences are tolerated


Conflictual / adversarial
Politics painted in stark contrasts — right and wrong — with emphasis on the triumph of one side over the other




For Lijphart (1999), consensual political culture produces “kinder and gentler” policies than majoritarian political cultures.



And the link runs both ways: consensual culture goes with consensual institutions, adversarial culture with majoritarian institutions.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 96; Lijphart (1999, p. 305).
Hold this slide for Session 9 — Lijphart’s “Constitutional Choices for New Democracies” is the November 5 article, and this is its cultural premise.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Richardson: fair share and fair play
text:
Richardson: fair share and fair play
Bradley Richardson (1984), on Japanese political culture, draws the same contrast at the level of what citizens think fairness is.







Fair share (consensual)
What matters is that all share equally in the outcome


Fair play (adversarial)
No matter the outcome, if the game was played fairly the result is legitimate





This is a usable test. Ask of any political system: when people call an outcome unjust, are they objecting to the distribution or to the procedure?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The European redefinitions
Scholars took a broader view: political culture as what lets people make sense of politics, not as attitudes toward one particular system.







Elkins & Simeon (1979)
A set of assumptions; a “mind set” that limits attention to less than the full range of logically possible behaviours, problems and solutions


Robertson (1985)
“The totality of ideas and attitudes towards authority, discipline, governmental responsibilities and entitlements”


Rose (1980)
Sets of “values, beliefs and emotions,” taken for granted, which “give meaning to politics”


Kavanagh (1985)
Disposes members to regard certain political behaviour and institutions as “normal” and others as “abnormal”


Topf (1989)
Attitudes as “expressions of values, or better, of positions in the moral order, constitutive of the political culture”


Welch (1993)
Not assumptions but resources — images, symbols, myths, traditions people draw on to make sense of their predicament




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 96–98.
Don’t drill the names. Drill the shift: from attitudes about a system to the equipment people use to interpret any system. The second version is detachable from institutions, which is what the critics demanded — and it is also vaguer, which is what Lijphart warned about. The field traded one problem for the other.
The Elkins and Simeon formulation is the one to keep: choices from a restricted set “remain below the threshold of consciousness, because they seldom encounter individuals who take for granted quite different assumptions” (1979, p. 128).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Criticism 2: is culture a cause or a result?
text:
Criticism 2: is culture a cause or a result?
Carole Pateman (1971): if political orientations are an integral part of the political system, attitudes can exist only in relation to a specific set of institutions.


Then political culture cannot be an independent variable, because it cannot be separated from the institutional context in which it exists.



Brian Barry goes further. Political culture is merely “reasonable expectations founded on common experience” of the existing system:

“Obviously, if this interpretation is correct, there are no grounds for saying that the correlation arises from the conduciveness of the ‘civic culture’ to ‘democracy’, but rather for the unexciting conclusion that ‘democracy’ produces the ‘civic culture’.”
Barry 1978, pp. 51–52


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 98–99; Barry (1978, pp. 51–52); Pateman (1971, 1980).
This is the single most transferable idea in the chapter: reverse causation. Name it as such.
Marxist critics such as Jerzy Wiatr (1980) point in the same direction, to the causal influence of social and economic realities on political culture. Pateman adds that the argument “neglects the association between class and participation and implies that social status is irrelevant” (1980, p. 84).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: Barry’s objection
Barry’s claim that “democracy produces the civic culture” is best described as:

A measurement-validity problem
A reverse-causation problem
A selection-bias problem
A concept-stretching problem



Reverse causation. The correlation is not in dispute — what is in dispute is which way the arrow points, and Barry argues the civic culture is the residue of living under democracy rather than its cause.


[Key] Option 2. Concept stretching is Lijphart’s separate objection, and measurement validity is the later Clarke et al. critique of Inglehart’s index — both appear in this chapter, which is why they make good distractors.
Push it one step: what evidence would separate the two stories? Over-time data on attitudes in countries that democratize later, which is exactly the design the World Values Survey eventually made possible.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Lijphart’s defence, and a smaller claim
text:
Lijphart’s defence, and a smaller claim
Lijphart (1980) replies that the question is wrongly posed: it is a mistake to think of culture and structure in either/or terms.

Structures clearly affect political culture
Culture clearly affects which structures emerge
They are inherently linked and occur simultaneously


Elkins and Simeon (1979) offer the more modest repair: most studies fail to control for other factors.

Political culture should not be the explanation of first resort but of last resort — what social, economic and political structures cannot explain. It is the variation in the dependent variable that structural factors leave over.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 99–100.
The last-resort rule is methodologically respectable and intellectually deflating at once, and it is worth putting that tension to the class. It does protect against lazy culturalism. It also guarantees that culture can never be tested directly, only credited with a residual.
For their dossiers, the rule is a discipline: a team that reaches for “the political culture there is different” before exhausting institutional and economic explanations has skipped the work.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Criticism 3: where do political cultures come from?
text:
Criticism 3: where do political cultures come from?
Almond and Verba show correlations between attitudes and educational attainment, implying political culture is produced by individuals and institutions together.


But they never explain how, beyond invoking political socialization
And Pateman (1980): socialization only takes an active role if there are tensions between people’s independently generated orientations and how the system actually works




Definition problems, plus the independence problem, plus no account of production — together these produced a decline in interest in the concept in comparative politics.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: The renaissance

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Why the concept came back
At the end of the 1980s, renewed interest in the United States — Europe had never abandoned it.

Real-world puzzles no structural account could handle: radical Islamic fundamentalism; the extraordinary modernization of several East Asian countries
The collapse of the Soviet Union and of communism in Central and Eastern Europe — how had changing political cultures brought communism down?
Consolidation: the congruence of culture with institutions as a prerequisite for new democracies (Linz and Stepan 1996; Rose, Mishler and Haerpfer 1998; Diamond 1999)



Putnam (1993), Making Democracy Work, on the republican virtues — civic community, tolerance, cooperation, solidarity.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 100–101.
Note the pattern, because it recurs in the discipline: a concept returns not because its logical problems were solved but because events arrived that rival concepts could not explain.
Inglehart’s own definition is the detached one: culture is “a system of common basic values that help shape the behavior of the people in a given society” (1997, p. 217) — values and attitudes independent of particular political structures.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Inglehart: post-materialism
As in Maslow’s hierarchy of needs, individuals pursue goals in hierarchical order — material needs first, non-material needs as material ones are satisfied.








Scarcity
Emphasis on economic growth and security — strong national defence, “law and order”


Affluence
Shift to personal freedom, political participation, quality of life, a clean environment






And not a passing mood: through socialization, post-material orientations transfer to subsequent generations and become a stable value system rather than a volatile attitude.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The growth that made the shift possible
text:
The growth that made the shift possible
Average annual growth in income per capita, 1945–1970:

That growth, plus the extensive welfare state, produced unprecedented economic security — and security is the mechanism by which Inglehart’s value shift occurs.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The four-item index
Inglehart’s measure, built on American National Election Studies data. Respondents choose their first and then their second most desirable national goal:

Maintaining order in the nation
Giving the people more say in important political decisions
Fighting rising prices
Protecting freedom of speech



(1) and (3) → pure materialists · (2) and (4) → post-materialists
Inglehart 1971, p. 94



World Values Survey (2000) — highest post-materialist shares: Australia 35%, Austria 30%, Canada 29%, United States 25%.

[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 102–103; Inglehart (1971, p. 94); Inglehart et al. (2004, p. 384).
Read the four items aloud and have students answer privately before revealing the coding. Then ask what the index assumes: that items 1 and 3 are the economic-and-security pair, and 2 and 4 the autonomy pair. The critique on a later slide is an attack on exactly that assumption.
Subsequent variations appear in the General Social Survey, the World Values Survey and elsewhere.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The new values of the 1990s
By the 1990s the shift had produced a distinct set of political values:

The diminishing effectiveness and acceptability of bureaucratic authority — small is better
A growing emphasis on individual freedom and emotional experience, and the questioning of all forms of authority
The diminishing prestige of science, technology and rationality, and a re-embrace of religion



That third item is the one that generates Table 4.2: religion returning as a basis of authority cross-cuts the materialist/post-materialist axis rather than lying along it.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Table 4.2 · Material versus post-material values by authority type
text:
Table 4.2 · Material versus post-material values by authority type

Ishiyama, Table 4.2








Traditional values(materialist)
Postmodern values(post-materialist)




Rational / legal / secular(emphasis on state authority)
Post-communist Eastern Europe, China, Japan (somewhat)
Northern Europe, Canada (increasingly Japan)


Traditional authority(e.g. religion)
Poland, most of the developing world
Italy, Spain, Mexico, Argentina, the US (a borderline case), Ireland




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, Table 4.2; after Weber (1947) on patterns of authority and Inglehart.
The rows come from Weber’s distinction between rational-legal and traditional bases of state authority: people obey either because it is in their self-interest to do so, or because that is how it has always been — often because authority rests on religious values. The columns are Inglehart’s value axis. Two dimensions, four cells.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Reading Table 4.2

Secular + materialist — the post-communist states, from communism’s secular legacy plus relatively lower development than the West. China likewise. Poland is the exception, where Catholicism is a powerful legitimizing force
Secular + post-materialist — most of northern Europe, Canada, and to some extent the US. Japan is a borderline case: secular, and increasingly post-materialist
Traditional + materialist — most of the developing world
Traditional + post-materialist — Catholic southern Europe, Latin America, and arguably the US, given the strong influence of religion on its politics



The payoff for democracy: where traditional authority predominates, expect a less participatory impulse — close to Almond and Verba’s subject culture. Add materialist values and you get something less than participatory democracy.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 104–105.
The US appears twice and students will object. Say why: Ishiyama treats it as a borderline case on the authority dimension precisely because religion weighs unusually heavily in American politics for a wealthy secular-legal state. A case that resists the typology is a finding, not an error.
The chapter’s own conclusion is the one to write down: economic development and post-material values may lead to democracy, but the quality of that democracy, or its type, is powerfully affected by the legacy of past authority patterns.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Postmodernization
Inglehart (1997) generalizes beyond post-materialism: western industrial democracies have entered a new phase.

“In the postmodernization phase of development, emphasis shifts from maximizing economic gains to maximizing subjective well-being.” (p. 86)


The post-materialist shift is “only one part of a broader shift toward postmodern values, involving changing orientations towards politics, work, family life, religion, and sexual behavior” (p. 132).



New priorities follow: environmental protection, abortion, ethnic diversity, women’s issues, gay rights (p. 247).


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 105–106; Inglehart (1997).
Micro-level evidence Ishiyama cites for the West: class-based cleavages have weakened (Huckfeldt and Kohfeld 1989; Ladd and Hadley 1975), and social and cultural issues have moved to the forefront of American politics ahead of bread-and-butter economics (Inglehart and Abramson 1994).
The party-level illustration is the better teaching case. Before WWII the Social Democratic/Labour Left fought over wages, the economic rights of the working classes, and ownership of the means of production. After the post-war boom came a “greening” of the European Left, accelerating in the 1990s: openness, accountability, public-private partnership, smaller government, individual rights. Ishiyama reads Blairism, and the merger that produced the Dutch GroenLinks, in this light.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The measurement critique
Critics (Flanagan 1982; Clarke and Dutt 1991; Duch and Taylor 1993, 1994) attack the four-item index itself.
Clarke et al. (1999, p. 637): substituting an unemployment statement for the standard inflation statement “has major consequences for the classification of respondents as materialist or postmaterialist.”

“When inflation is not a salient economic problem, respondents eschew the rising prices item but are forced by the format to choose one of the remaining three, none of which deals with other economic concerns they may have. Respondents who do not select the prices item have a zero probability of being classified as materialist.”



The deeper worry: post-materialism may not be a stable value set at all, but a response to conditions — post-materialist in good times, materialist in downturns or under security threat.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 106–107; Clarke et al. (1999, p. 637).
Note where this lands: back at Barry’s objection. If values track economic conditions, then culture again lacks an independent effect beyond economic and material circumstances — the same criticism made of Almond and Verba thirty years earlier.
Methodologically this is a forced-choice instrument problem, and it generalizes. Ask students what happens to any ranking scale when the item that would capture a respondent’s real concern is simply not on the list.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: what is the Clarke et al. critique?
text:
Check: what is the Clarke et al. critique?
The Clarke et al. (1999) objection to Inglehart’s index is that:

The sample was unrepresentative
The forced-choice format makes classification depend on which items are offered
Post-materialism was measured in too few countries
Respondents misunderstood the question wording



The forced-choice format. Swap the inflation item for an unemployment item and respondents get reclassified — so the measure is partly an artefact of the instrument, and partly of current economic conditions.


[Key] Option 2. This item is doing double duty: it tests the chapter, and it tests whether students can tell a measurement problem from a sampling problem. Both appear in their own dossier work.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 4: Ethnic politics and nationalism

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Why ethnicity enters a chapter on culture
text:
Why ethnicity enters a chapter on culture
As political culture came to mean a set of values through which politics is interpreted, it moved closer to the other shortcuts people use to make sense of politics.


In the era of multiculturalism, culture became equated with ethnicity
In the US especially, multiculturalism is used interchangeably with inter-ethnic or inter-racial relations




Ishiyama’s justification is the close relationship between cultural and ethnic identities — but notice that an equation has quietly been made, and it is worth asking whether it holds.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
What is “ethnicity”?
Glazer and Moynihan (1975, p. 1) remarked that “ethnicity seems to be a new term” — but the root is very old.

From the Greek ethnos, originally meaning “heathen” or “pagan”
Largely ignored by social science, with the notable exception of Max Weber



Two broad contemporary approaches: primordial and constructivist.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Primordialism
Ethnicity is a natural phenomenon, present throughout human history; modern ethnic groups have roots extending far into the past. Groups are defined by kinship and bloodlines.







Essentialist
The extreme version: ethnic groups are not merely historical but naturally occurring. Consistent with early-twentieth-century scientific racialism — the intellectual soil of eugenics and National Socialism (Smith 1999, pp. 4–7)


Historical
Ethnic groups are historical entities, extensions of kinship but more than kinship, defined by cultural signs — language, religion, traditions — that symbolize biological unity





Clifford Geertz (1973): ethnicity may not be a biological condition, but what matters is that humans perceive it as such — making it an objective condition, as real as if it were physical.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 108–109.
The Geertz move is subtle and students flatten it. He is not saying ethnicity is biologically real; he is saying the belief has real consequences, which is a sociological claim, not a genetic one. It is the hinge between the two approaches rather than a pure primordialist position.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Constructivism
Ethnicity and ethnic identity are malleable and flexible.

Weber: a “subjective belief” in “common descent. Whether or not an objective blood relationship exists” (1978, p. 389)
Schildkrout (1979, p. 184): the minimal definition is “the idea of common provenance, recruitment primarily through kinship, and a notion of distinctiveness, whether or not this consists of a unique inventory of cultural traits”
Benedict Anderson (1991): nations as imagined communities — socially constructed products of human interaction, maintained for instrumental reasons: to validate governance, to bind a community


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 109–110; Weber (1978, p. 389, cited in Guibernau and Rex 1997, p. 3); see also Horowitz (1985), Smith (1986), Schildkrout (1974).
Weber appears on both halves of this chapter — the Protestant ethic at the start and the subjective definition of ethnicity here. Worth pointing out: the same author is cited by the culturalists and by the constructivists.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The modernist variant
A related claim: ethnicity is purely a modern invention, appearing only in the modern period of world history.

Marx and Engels — nations as a primarily bourgeois construct that would wither away after the collapse of capitalism
Hobsbawm (1990) — before the industrial era there was no ideal of politicized ethnic identities; these were created by modernization
Karl Deutsch (1953) — same point from the communications side



Note what this does to the causal story: if modernization creates politicized ethnicity, then ethnic conflict is not a survival from the past but a product of development.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, p. 110; Deutsch (1953); Hobsbawm (1990).
Deutsch is the same author from Chapter 3 — social mobilization. Make the link: mobilization pulls people out of local worlds into national communication networks, and that is exactly when ethnic difference becomes politically legible. This is the strongest bridge in the chapter back to last week.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Nationalism as an ideology
Ethnicity can express itself politically in many ways. In the modern era many ethnic conflicts are couched as nationalist struggles — but, as Ishiyama and Breuning (1998) note, not all ethnopolitics is nationalistic.


Nationalism is a socio-political ideology whose core principles are:

Popular sovereignty — a people must have a state
The glorification of the community


Nationalists see the establishment and protection of the nation state as the highest political goal.




And if nationalism is an ideology like any other, there can be different types of it — some ethnic, some not.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Greenfeld’s two dimensions
Greenfeld (1992) classifies nationalisms along two questions:


What is the nation? A collection of individuals (individualism), or a collective entity that is more than the sum of its parts (collectivism)?
Who belongs to the nation? Does citizenship alone qualify (civic), or is membership defined by blood (ethnic)?



These will importantly affect not only whether democracy emerges, but what form it takes if it does.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Table 4.3 · Types of nationalism

Ishiyama, Table 4.3








Civic
Ethnic




Individualism
Individualist / civic (US)
Not possible


Collectivism
Collectivist / civic (France)
Collectivist / ethnic (most of Eastern Europe)





Four cells, three logical types. One combination cannot exist — and working out why is the point of the table.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, Table 4.3, after Greenfeld (1992).
Do not give away the empty cell. Put the table up and ask the class why individualist/ethnic is impossible before you say anything. The next slide is the answer.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Reading Table 4.3

Individualist / civic — the US. The nation is a collection of individuals; membership rests (in theory) on allegiance to a set of principles enshrined in the Constitution. Individual rights are often held above the interests of the collective
Collectivist / civic — France. The nation is something more than a collection of individuals — La Belle France — yet who may belong is based on allegiance and, at least in principle, not on blood
Collectivist / ethnic — much of Central and Eastern Europe. The nation is a collective unit and membership is defined by blood and kinship



The third type is the most common and the most problematic for consolidating democracy: collective interests outrank individual rights, and blood descent gives outgroups no route into the national community. Under social and economic stress this breeds intolerance, incivility, and unwillingness to compromise with “outsiders.”


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 111–112; Greenfeld (1992).
The empty cell: defining the nation as a collection of individuals who are free to belong by allegiance is logically at odds with restricting membership by descent. Individualism makes membership a matter of the individual’s own commitment; ethnic membership makes it a matter of inheritance. The two criteria cannot both govern entry.
Caution students against reading the US cell as a description of American practice. Ishiyama writes “in theory” and means it; the gap between the civic self-description and the actual history of who counted is itself a comparative research question.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: why is one cell empty?
text:
Check: why is one cell empty?
Why does Greenfeld’s typology hold that individualist / ethnic nationalism is not possible?

No such country has yet been observed
Individualism makes belonging a matter of the individual’s own allegiance, which contradicts membership by inheritance
Ethnic nations are always large, and large nations are collectivist
Individualism and ethnicity are measured on the same dimension



Option 2. The exclusion is logical, not empirical — the two dimensions give contradictory answers to the question of how a person comes to belong.


[Key] Option 2. Option 1 is the trap, and a revealing one: students treat an empty cell in a typology as a gap in the data. It is worth stating the general rule — a typology’s empty cells are claims about what can be, and they are refuted by argument, not by searching harder for a case.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 5: Does diversity endanger democracy?

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The pessimistic tradition







J. S. Mill (1958, p. 230)
“Free institutions are next to impossible in a country made up of different nationalities” — multinational societies as a continuous threat to social peace


Almond (1956)
The probability of violent conflict rises as a function of ethnic heterogeneity


Powell (1982)
A negative relationship between ethnic fractionalization and governmental stability, civil peace, and the prospects for democracy


Rabushka & Shepsle (1972)
Ethnic divisions are inimical to democracy — and democratic competition exacerbates ethnic conflict through ethnic outbidding by ethnic elites and their organizations


Reilly (2003)
Ethnic parties appeal specifically on ethnicity, so their emergence has a centrifugal effect — especially harmful where democratic institutions are fragile





The mechanism in the outbidding model: competing for the ethnic vote means mobilizing the group, and the cheapest way to mobilize is inflammatory “us versus them” rhetoric.


[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 112–114.
Even the pessimists mostly stop short of impossibility. David Welch’s formulation is the fair statement of the position: “establishing and sustaining democratic institutions in ethnically divided societies is a difficult task” (1993, p. 55).
Horowitz’s observation is the one students remember: “Democracy has progressed furthest in those East European countries that have the fewest serious ethnic cleavages (Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Poland) and progressed more slowly or not at all in those that are deeply divided (Slovakia, Bulgaria, Romania, and of course the former Yugoslavia)” (1993, p. 19).
Ask what is wrong with that as evidence. It is a correlation across a handful of cases with no control for the economic and institutional differences that also distinguish them — which is Lijphart’s many-variables, few-cases problem in the wild.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
The revisionists







Fearon & Laitin (1996)
Ethnic heterogeneity does not predispose societies to conflict, civil war, or democratic collapse. Population size and the proportion of mountainous terrain matter far more to civil conflict than fractionalization


Horowitz (1985, 1993)
Conflict follows from diversity only at very high or very low fractionalization. Risk is highest where a majority group faces a very sizeable minority — Sinhalese and Tamils in Sri Lanka; Fijians and ethnic Indians in Fiji


Collier & Hoeffler (1998)
“Highly fractionalized societies are no more prone to war than highly homogeneous ones. The danger of civil war arises when the society is polarized into two groups”


Montalvo & Reynal-Querol (2005)
Polarization, not fractionalization, explains conflict


Reilly (2000)
In Papua New Guinea, so many groups that no one group could monopolize power — diversity promoted tolerance and coalition politics


Hardgrave (1993)
A similar argument for peace and democracy in India




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 114–115.
Fearon and Laitin’s mountains result is worth dwelling on for a minute, because it is a lesson in research design rather than a fact about mountains: a variable that correlates with conflict can be displaced entirely once a plausible rival is measured properly.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Fractionalization is not polarization

Fractionalization — how many groups there are, and how evenly the population divides among them.
Polarization — how far the distribution approaches two groups of comparable size facing one another.



Many small groups: high fractionalization, low polarization — and no group can rule alone
One majority against one sizeable minority: moderate fractionalization, high polarization — and the worst risk




This is why the early literature kept finding a relationship and the later literature kept failing to: they were measuring different things.


Connect to Chapter 7 and Session 7’s reading on electoral systems. Whether a cleavage structure becomes two blocs or many is partly an institutional choice, not only a demographic fact.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: It depends on institutions and elites
text:
It depends on institutions and elites
The recent literature treats ethnic cleavages as cost-effective strategic resources for group formation, interest definition and collective action (Fearon and Laitin 2003; Birnir 2007; Chandra 2004; Posner 2004), and makes the effect conditional.







Consociationalists
Represent groups broadly and you integrate subcultures into the political game. Securing minority representation integrates disaffected groups, which moderates their demands (Lorwin 1971; Nordlinger 1972; Daalder 1974; McRae 1974; Lijphart 1977)


Cohen (1997, p. 613)
“By making institutions more accessible and making ethnic cleavages more explicit, ethnic groups will engage in more frequent but less intense conflict”


Chandra (2004, 2005)
Attacks outbidding directly: institutions that restrict ethnic politics “to a single dimension destabilize democracy, whereas institutions that foster multiple dimensions of ethnic identity can sustain it” (2005, p. 236)


Birnir (2007)
Ethnic identity is a stable but flexible information shortcut; ethnic parties as “attractors” prefer peaceful routes to power. Violence follows from denial of access to the executive, not from the ethnification of politics




[Sources] Ishiyama ch. 4, pp. 115–117.
Birnir’s logic is worth spelling out because it is a clean piece of reasoning: like all parties, ethnic parties seek leverage for a constituency; voters who use ethnic identity as a shortcut prefer parties that act for that constituency; so the attractor has a strong incentive to reach the executive, and the peaceful route is the reliable one. The deviation to be explained is therefore not peace but exclusion.
Her question is the good exam question: why do members of some ethnic groups peacefully support their group in electoral politics while others exit and turn to protest and violence? Her answer is access.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: fractionalization or polarization?
Collier and Hoeffler (1998) and Montalvo and Reynal-Querol (2005) conclude that civil conflict is best predicted by:

The number of ethnic groups
The degree of polarization into two opposed groups
The size of the largest ethnic group
The ratio of ethnic to religious cleavages



Polarization. Highly fractionalized societies are no more prone to war than highly homogeneous ones — the danger comes from a two-bloc structure, which is why Reilly’s Papua New Guinea, with very many groups, looks peaceful rather than explosive.


[Key] Option 2. Option 1 is the whole early literature’s answer, which is what makes it a good distractor — students who learned the pessimistic tradition first will pick it.
The payoff question: Horowitz’s “very high or very low fractionalization” claim and the polarization claim are close to the same claim stated in different vocabulary. Ask whether they are, and what data would distinguish them.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Where this leaves the argument

Ishiyama’s own summing up: there is little question that culture and ethnopolitics have some kind of effect — while the debate over whether culture is independent, and whether diversity kills democracy, remains open.


Two conclusions he does commit to:

Where political cultures value tolerance, moderation, compromise and civility, democracy is easier to develop
Deeply divided societies face greater challenges, but democracy is not impossible there




What is decisive is how democratic institutions are designed, and whether they fit a particular ethnic and cultural context — as in a place as divided as Iraq.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s article: Posner (2004)
Posner, “The Political Salience of Cultural Difference” — cited in this chapter among the contingent accounts, and the reason it belongs beside it.

The Chewa and Tumbuka straddle the Zambia–Malawi border: the same cultural difference, the same colonial-era history
In Malawi they are political adversaries; in Zambia they are allies
The difference is not the cleavage but the political arena: group size relative to the national electorate determines whether the difference is a useful coalitional building block



Read it as a design as much as an argument — a natural experiment that holds culture constant and varies the arena, which is how you test whether identity is politically salient rather than merely present.


Posner is the Session 5 article. Two reasons to spend time on it.
First, substance: it is the sharpest available answer to this chapter’s central question — identities become political when political entrepreneurs find them useful at the scale at which they must build a coalition. That is the constructivist and institutionalist answer rolled together.
Second, method: it is a most-similar-systems design of the kind Lijphart recommended in Session 1, and students should be able to name it as such without prompting by now. Ask what is held constant, what varies, and what the inference rests on.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
For your dossier
Round 2 — the context diagnosis — asks explicitly for cleavages. This chapter supplies the vocabulary and, more usefully, the warnings.
Four things to try this week:

Describe your focal country’s cleavage structure in terms of fractionalization and polarization. They can point in opposite directions, and the difference is often the whole story
Place its nationalism in Table 4.3. If the collectivist/ethnic cell fits, say what that predicts about who can enter the political community
Before writing “the political culture there is different,” apply the Elkins and Simeon rule: have you ruled out institutional and economic explanations first?
Watch for Barry’s objection in your own draft. If your evidence for a civic culture is that the country is democratic, you have assumed your conclusion

text:
For next session

Ishiyama, Chapter 6, pp. 134–156
Levitsky and Way, “Linkage versus Leverage”

Chapters 3 and 4 both explained democracy from the inside. Chapter 6 asks how much of it was ever decided inside the country at all.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Today’s puzzle

Why did some states enter the twentieth century with durable democratic institutions while others remained authoritarian or experienced democratic breakdown?


Two readings give us different parts of an answer:

Ishiyama offers a historical explanation across six countries
Lijphart shows how to evaluate comparisons when cases are few and causes are many


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Comparative Politics, Chapter 2. - Lijphart, “Comparative Politics and the Comparative Method” (1971), pp. 682–693.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Learning goals
By the end of class, you should be able to:

Distinguish a democratic threshold from degrees of polyarchy
Explain Ishiyama’s three historical conditions for democratization
Compare the six country trajectories using common questions
Diagnose the “many variables, small number of cases” problem
Turn a historical narrative into a testable comparative claim

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Opening comparison


Britain

Parliament constrained the Crown before industrialization
Landed elites became commercially oriented
Political inclusion widened gradually


Russia

Autocracy remained dominant
Serfdom and elite dependence persisted
Reform arrived late and was reversed




Cold-call question: Which difference looks most causally important, and what evidence would change your mind?


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, country discussions of Britain and Russia.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Check: why did wool matter?
Rising Mediterranean demand for English wool changed English politics. Through what mechanism?

Wool revenue let the Crown govern without summoning Parliament
Wool needs much land and little labour, so landlords enclosed the commons
Wool profits paid for the standing army the Stuarts wanted
The wool trade imported Continental ideas about representation



The second. The asymmetry is the whole mechanism: land mattered, labour did not — so the peasantry was displaced and the nobility became commercial.


[Key] The second. This separates students who followed the causal chain from those who retain only “wool was important.”
The first option inverts the political outcome — in England the Crown lost that struggle. The third attaches real Stuart-era material to the wrong mechanism. Both are plausible enough to be worth naming aloud.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 1: The outcome to explain

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Democracy has more than one definition
text:
Democracy has more than one definition


Schumpeter
Democracy is a method for selecting leaders through a competitive struggle for votes.
This is a narrow, procedural definition.

Held
Democracy requires political equality among members of the political community.
This is a more demanding standard.


The definition determines which cases count as democratic.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of Schumpeter and Held.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Dahl’s polyarchy
Dahl treats democracy as an ideal and uses polyarchy for real political systems.


Competition

Elected officials
Free and fair elections
Freedom of expression
Alternative information
Independent associations


Participation

Broad suffrage
Broad eligibility for office
Equal consideration of preferences



Countries may improve on one dimension without improving equally on the other.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, summary of Dahl (1989).

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
A democratic threshold
For the study of transitions, Ishiyama uses four minimum components drawn from Linz and Stepan and from Rose, Mishler, and Haerpfer.







Component
Diagnostic question




Rule of law
Are rulers bound by law?


Civil society
Can groups organize independently of the state?


Free and fair elections
Is there meaningful competition for office?


Accountability
Must governing officials answer for their actions?




No single component is sufficient. The combination identifies whether a regime has crossed a democratic threshold.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of the minimal definition of democracy.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Two measures answer different questions








Concept
What it measures
Best question




Minimal democracy
A categorical threshold
Has the regime become democratic?


Polyarchy
Degrees of competition and participation
How democratic is the regime?





Democratization first establishes the minimum institutions, then can deepen competition and participation.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: why does Dahl need a second word?
text:
Check: why does Dahl need a second word?
Dahl reserves democracy for an ideal type and calls real systems polyarchies. Why?

Because existing democracies differ from one another
Because no actual system fully approximates the ideal
Because the term applies only after a completed transition



The second. The ideal is a standard, not a description — so every real case falls short of it, and the question becomes by how much.


[Key] The second option. The common error is the first: students who remember that polyarchies vary along competition and participation mistake a consequence of the term for its reason. The third describes the minimal-threshold approach (Linz and Stepan), not Dahl.
Ask for hands before revealing. If the room splits between one and two, that split is the teaching moment.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 2: Ishiyama’s historical argument

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Industrialization as a political shock
Industrialization changes more than production.

New classes seek political influence
Cities and markets unsettle older hierarchies
States face demands for representation and protection
Existing institutions must absorb or repress conflict



Ishiyama treats industrialization as a storm. The outcome depends partly on the political vessel constructed before the storm arrived.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, historical approach and ship metaphor.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Sequence is the central mechanism


Before
National identity, social order, and limits on rulers develop unevenly.

During
Industrialization creates new wealth, classes, conflicts, and demands.

After
Institutions incorporate new groups, break down, or harden into authoritarian rule.


The same economic shock can therefore produce different political outcomes.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Three historical conditions

Political national identity existed before industrialization
Accountability and rule of law constrained rulers before industrialization
The feudal or old social order had been transformed before industrialization



The argument is configurational. The conditions reinforce each other rather than operating as isolated causes.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, three questions organizing the six cases.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: which one is not on the list?
text:
Check: which one is not on the list?
Ishiyama organizes all six cases around three conditions established before industrialization. Which of these is not one of them?

A mass national identity
Accountability and the rule of law
The old social order swept away
An industrial working class organized into parties



The fourth. It sounds like something a chapter about industrialization ought to ask — which is exactly why it is worth naming as absent.


[Key] The fourth. Party organization of the working class is not among the three. The point is not trivia: the three conditions are all pre-industrial, and the chapter’s whole argument is that what mattered had already happened before the shock arrived. A condition defined by industrial society could not do that work.
Have them write the three down here. Round 2 asks their team to answer versions of all three about their focal country.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Political national identity
Ishiyama distinguishes cultural community from political unity.







Concept
Basis of membership




Kulturnation
Shared language, culture, religion, or ancestry


Staatsnation
Shared political institutions and a recognized political community





Cultural homogeneity does not automatically produce political integration. Japan was relatively homogeneous, yet its modern political identity had to be constructed.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, discussion of cultural and political nationhood.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Accountability before mass politics
The issue is not whether a country already had universal suffrage.
The issue is whether institutions had already established that:

Rulers could be constrained
Revenue and law required bargaining
Organized interests could act outside the state
Political conflict could occur within accepted institutions


Early accountability provided channels through which later demands could enter politics.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Transformation of the old order
A landed elite may respond to economic change in different ways.


Transformed elite

Wealth becomes commercial
Status depends less on hereditary privilege
Elites can bargain within representative institutions


Persistent old order

Land and labor remain coercively organized
Elites depend on autocratic protection
New groups threaten established privilege



The second path makes democratic inclusion more threatening to incumbent elites.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, use of Barrington Moore and the transformation of feudalism.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: The argument as a causal chain
text:
The argument as a causal chain








Stage
Historical question
Expected consequence




Community
Is there an accepted political nation?
Conflict stays within a shared polity


Constraint
Are rulers accountable under law?
New demands enter established channels


Social order
Has hereditary privilege been transformed?
Elites can tolerate broader participation


Industrial shock
How intense is social disruption?
Earlier arrangements face a stress test


Outcome
Are conflict and inclusion institutionalized?
Democracy, instability, or authoritarianism




[Sources] - Analytical reconstruction from Ishiyama, Chapter 2.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text: Part 3: Six trajectories

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Britain

Political centralization and national integration developed early
The wool economy and enclosure weakened the traditional peasantry
Landed elites became commercially oriented
Parliament defeated royal absolutism and secured rule-bound bargaining
Suffrage expanded within an already accepted institutional arena



Democratization widened access to the stadium. It did not require constructing a new stadium during the crisis.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Britain section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
France

Absolutism subordinated nobles and weakened independent accountability
Labor-intensive agriculture preserved a large peasantry
The Revolution destroyed noble privilege but did not produce immediate institutional consensus
New social demands repeatedly met resistance outside stable channels
Democratic development lurched through revolution, reaction, and constitutional redesign


France shows partial preparation followed by repeated institutional rupture.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, France section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
section: Check: why did French feudalism survive?
text:
Check: why did French feudalism survive?
England and France faced the same commercial opening. France did not transform. Why not?

The Revolution destroyed the nobility before commercial agriculture could develop
France entered international trade later, delaying commercial pressure
French production was labour-intensive, so landlords kept peasants rather than shedding them
There was no commercial demand for French agricultural products



The third. Viniculture and similar crops needed hands on the land. Same pressure, opposite incentive, opposite outcome.


[Key] The third. The first reverses the sequence — the Revolution came after the failure to transform, and Ishiyama is explicit that it destroyed the nobility while strengthening the peasantry. The fourth is simply false in the chapter: demand rose.
This is the pair’s payoff. Ask why the comparison is informative at all, and the answer is that the crop is the only thing that differs in the relevant respect.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
United States

Colonial assemblies established traditions of representation and accountability
The country lacked European feudalism
A unified political nation remained contested by sectional identity
Slavery sustained hereditary racial privilege in the South
Civil War settled the supremacy of the national state through violence



Institutions arrived early, but national political integration arrived late.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, United States section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Germany

Political fragmentation persisted into the nineteenth century
The Junker elite retained power in Prussia
Unification occurred through authoritarian state-building and war
Industrialization outpaced democratization
Weimar inherited deep cleavages, weak democratic commitment, war debt, and severe crisis


Rapid state formation did not produce an equally rapid democratic settlement.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Germany section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Japan

Tokugawa rule ended civil conflict but preserved decentralized feudal structures
Meiji leaders constructed political identity around loyalty to the emperor
The state directed modernization under external pressure
Old domains and military traditions were adapted rather than fully displaced
Durable democracy followed defeat and postwar institutional reconstruction


Japan separates cultural homogeneity from democratic political integration.

[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Japan section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Russia

Empire preceded a distinct modern national political community
Loyalty centered on the Tsar and the state
Autocracy destroyed or subordinated alternative centers of power
Serfdom and a dependent nobility persisted
Reform after 1905 left the Tsar’s veto and dissolution powers intact
War and state collapse opened the path to revolution rather than democracy



Russia is Ishiyama’s sharpest contrast with Britain across all three historical conditions.


[Sources] - Ishiyama, Chapter 2, Russia section.

title: PSCI 3350.001 Comparative Politics
text:
Six cases on common dimensions











Case
Political identity before industrialization
Accountability before industrialization
Transformation of old order
Broad trajectory




Britain
Strong
Strong
Extensive
Gradual inclusion


France
Partial
Weak
Partial
Repeated rupture


United States
Contested
Strong
Mixed because of slavery
Integration through civil war


Germany
Weak
Weak

Authoritarian unification, fragile democracy


Japan
Constructed from above
Weak
